concept_summary: Einstein's 1905 analysis of a small sphere suspended in a stationary liquid gives a diffusion coefficient D that grows with absolute temperature T and falls with the liquid's dynamic viscosity eta and the sphere's radius a. For one axis, the mean-square displacement is MSD = 2*D*t and the root-mean-square displacement is RMS = sqrt(2*D*t). The lesson lets you vary T, eta, a and t and watch D, MSD and RMS update, so you can see that RMS grows as the square root of time and that doubling eta or a halves D.

controls.meaning: Time elapsed since the start of observation, in seconds; MSD and RMS grow with t while D does not depend on t.

equations.explanation: Einstein's diffusion expression for a sphere of radius P in a liquid of viscosity k, with R the gas constant and N the number of molecules per mole. The excerpt supplies this as an equation transcription from Section 3.
Teaching notation: write eta for the viscosity coefficient k, a for the sphere radius P, and k_B = R/N. This is a relabelling of the source expression, not a new physical claim.

Unit conversion used by the demo: with eta in mPa*s, a in micrometres and D in micrometre^2/s, the coefficient 0.01380649 combines 1e-3 Pa*s per mPa*s, 1e-6 m per micrometre, 1e12 micrometre^2 per m^2 and the modern exact k_B = 1.380649e-23 J/K. The decimal coefficient and the pi approximation are modern teaching/unit conversions, not numbers fitted by Einstein.

For motion along one axis, the mean of the squared displacements is 2*D*t and its square root is the root-mean-square displacement. Equation (11) of Section 4 gives lambda_x = sqrt(mean(x^2)) = sqrt(2*D*t).
Because RMS = sqrt(2*D*t), the mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time.

explanation_steps.body: Einstein's Section 3 expression for the diffusion coefficient of a small sphere in a stationary liquid is D = (R*T/N)/(6*pi*k*P), where k is the liquid's viscosity coefficient and P is the sphere's radius. The excerpt supplies this as an equation transcription. In this lesson we write eta for k, a for P, and k_B = R/N, so D = k_B*T/(6*pi*eta*a). D therefore rises with temperature and falls with viscosity and radius.
explanation_steps.heading: Where D comes from

explanation_steps.body: Section 4, equation (11) gives lambda_x = sqrt(mean(x^2)) = sqrt(2*D*t), and the preceding passage identifies this as the square root of the arithmetic mean of squared displacements along the x-axis. So the mean-square displacement along one axis is MSD = 2*D*t and the one-axis RMS is its square root. The prose excerpt states that the mean displacement is proportional to the square root of the time.
explanation_steps.heading: From D to one-axis RMS

explanation_steps.body: The demo converts units so that eta is entered in mPa*s, a in micrometres, and D comes out in micrometre^2/s: D = 0.01380649*T/(6*pi*eta*a). The coefficient 0.01380649 and the pi approximation are modern teaching/unit conversions, not numbers fitted by Einstein. All slider values are teaching examples, not a reproduction of any measurement.
explanation_steps.heading: Units and the converted coefficient

explorations.change: Set t = 0 s, then raise t to 1 s and to 4 s while keeping T = 300 K, eta = 1 mPa*s and a = 1 micrometre.
explorations.observe: At t = 0 the MSD and RMS read exactly 0 while D stays at its positive value. Going from t = 1 s to t = 4 s multiplies MSD by 4 but only doubles RMS.
explorations.why: MSD = 2*D*t is linear in t, so it vanishes at t = 0 and scales with t; RMS = sqrt(2*D*t) is the square root, so quadrupling t doubles RMS. D itself contains no t, so it cannot change with elapsed time.

explorations.change: Double eta from 1 to 2 mPa*s, then double a from 1 to 2 micrometres, each time at T = 300 K and t = 1 s.
explorations.observe: Each doubling halves D, and with t fixed it also halves MSD and divides RMS by sqrt(2).
explorations.why: D = 0.01380649*T/(6*pi*eta*a) has eta and a in the denominator, so D is inversely proportional to each. MSD and RMS inherit that dependence through 2*D*t.

explorations.change: Sweep t from 0 to 60 s on the line view while holding T, eta and a fixed.
explorations.observe: The plotted RMS curve rises steeply at first and then flattens, passing through the origin.
explorations.why: RMS = sqrt(2*D*t) is a square-root curve in t: its slope decreases as t grows, and it is zero at t = 0. This is the square-root-of-time behaviour quoted in the source.

teaching_simplifications: The decimal coefficient 0.01380649 and the pi approximation 3.141592653589793 are modern teaching/unit conversions, not numbers fitted by Einstein.
Writing eta for the viscosity coefficient k, a for the sphere radius P, and k_B = R/N is teaching notation, not a claim from the excerpt.
The modern exact value k_B = 1.380649e-23 J/K is supplied from NIST and is not quoted from the 1905 paper.
All slider values are teaching examples; the demo does not reproduce any measurement.
The demo treats D as constant in time and space and ignores particle inertia, gravity, boundaries and interactions between particles.

limitations: The demo is a toy calculation of D, MSD and RMS from four sliders; it does not simulate a particle trajectory and does not reproduce experimental data.

RMS is not the mean signed displacement, the mean absolute displacement, the total path length, or the three-dimensional RMS displacement; it is the square root of the mean squared displacement along one axis only.
The expression D = 0.01380649*T/(6*pi*eta*a) assumes a sphere in a stationary, unbounded liquid of uniform viscosity and temperature, with no inertia, gravity, wall effects or particle interactions.
The coefficient 0.01380649 and the pi approximation are modern unit conversions, so the numerical outputs are not values printed in the 1905 paper.
The line view sweeps t only; it does not show the distribution of displacements, only the single RMS value at each time.

title: Einstein 1905: Diffusion and One-Axis RMS Displacement of a Small Sphere

visualizations.title: One-axis RMS displacement versus elapsed time

why_it_matters: Einstein's 1905 result connects a directly observable random walk, the mean-square displacement of a suspended particle, to molecular-kinetic quantities through D = k_B*T/(6*pi*eta*a). It shows that measuring how far a particle wanders in a known liquid at a known temperature yields information about the molecular scale, and it makes the square-root-of-time growth of the mean displacement a testable prediction rather than a guess.
